events.title: PHP 7.0 released
events.summary: The PHP project released PHP 7.0 on December 3, 2015 — roughly doubling performance and adding scalar type hints and the spaceship operator.
events.about: PHP 7 revived the language after years on PHP 5: [WordPress], Laravel, and [Symfony] sites ran dramatically faster on the same hardware. Scalar types and return declarations brought optional static discipline without losing PHP's deploy-by-[FTP] simplicity.

narrative.whyChosen: PHP 7 was the performance reboot that kept PHP relevant against [Node] and [Python].
narrative.whyImportant: A 2× speedup on real workloads changed hosting economics for millions of sites.
narrative.problemSolved: PHP 5.6 was slow and aging; the ecosystem needed a breaking cleanup to modernize internals.

events.title: Swift open-sourced
events.summary: Apple open-sourced [Swift] on December 3, 2015 under the Apache 2.0 license — releasing the compiler, standard library, and [Swift].org governance model.
events.about: Open [Swift] let the language run on Linux servers, attracted outside contributors, and separated [Swift] from pure Apple platform lock-in. It enabled server-side [Swift] experiments and laid groundwork for [Swift] on Windows and cross-platform tooling.

narrative.whyChosen: Open-sourcing [Swift] was Apple's bid to make it a general-purpose language, not just an [iOS] detail.
narrative.whyImportant: Community governance and Linux support expanded where [Swift] could run.
narrative.problemSolved: [Swift] was tied to [Xcode]; server and open-source adopters needed a portable toolchain.

events.title: Perl 6.c 'Christmas' released
events.summary: The [Perl] 6 team shipped the 6.c 'Christmas' language release on December 25, 2015 — the first production-ready [Perl] 6 after 15 years of design.
events.about: [Perl] 6 (later renamed Raku) brought grammars, gradual typing, and concurrency primitives to the [Perl] family. The Christmas release marked the end of '[Perl] 6 is coming' jokes and gave the community a compiler (Rakudo) to build on.

narrative.whyChosen: After a decade and a half, [Perl] 6 finally shipped as a real language.
narrative.whyImportant: It proved long-running language redesigns could reach production, even if adoption stayed niche.
narrative.problemSolved: [Perl] 5 could not evolve radically without breaking its massive installed base.

events.title: Let's Encrypt public beta launched
events.summary: Let's Encrypt entered public beta on December 3, 2015 — offering free, automated [TLS] certificates via the ACME protocol.
events.about: Let's Encrypt's ACME [API] lets servers prove domain ownership and receive short-lived certificates without manual paperwork or fees. Certbot and other clients renew certs automatically — [HTTPS] went from a luxury to the default for blogs, APIs, and static sites. Example: `certbot --[nginx]` obtains and installs a certificate, then cron renews it before expiry.

narrative.whyChosen: Let's Encrypt removed cost and friction from deploying [HTTPS] at scale.
narrative.whyImportant: It drove encrypted-by-default web traffic and standardized automated certificate issuance.
narrative.problemSolved: [TLS] certificates were expensive and manual; most small sites stayed on plain [HTTP].

events.title: Sam Altman co-founds OpenAI
events.summary: [OpenAI] launched in December 2015 with Sam Altman as co-chair — a research lab aimed at safe artificial general intelligence.
events.about: [OpenAI] pivoted from nonprofit research to the [API] and [ChatGPT] products that triggered the [generative AI] boom. Altman became the public face of frontier model deployment and developer-facing [LLM] APIs.

narrative.whyChosen: [OpenAI] under Altman defined the consumer and [API] [LLM] era.
narrative.whyImportant: It moved frontier models from labs into everyday software products.
narrative.problemSolved: Powerful AI was locked in research without safe, accessible deployment paths.

events.title: Ilya Sutskever named OpenAI research director
events.summary: [OpenAI] launched on December 11, 2015 with Ilya Sutskever as research director — the AlexNet co-author who would lead [GPT] and [reasoning]-model breakthroughs.
events.about: Sutskever left Google Brain to co-found [OpenAI]'s research program. He oversaw the scaling laws work behind [GPT]-3, [ChatGPT], and later o1-style [reasoning] models before leaving to start Safe Superintelligence.

narrative.whyChosen: Sutskever defined [OpenAI]'s research direction from inception through the [LLM] era.
narrative.whyImportant: His leadership turned [transformer] scaling into consumer products.
narrative.problemSolved: Frontier AI needed a research chief who could bridge academic breakthroughs and product deployment.

events.title: Figma collaborative design tool launches
events.summary: Figma announced its invite-only preview release on December 3, 2015 — a browser-based [UI] design app with real-time multiplayer editing.
events.about: Figma replaced Sketch files emailed between designers and developers — components, variants, and dev-mode specs lived in one shared [URL]. Design systems, FigJam whiteboards, and plugins made it the default handoff layer between product design and frontend implementation.

narrative.whyChosen: Figma moved [UI] design from desktop files to multiplayer browser collaboration.
narrative.whyImportant: Real-time co-editing and shared libraries reshaped design-dev workflows.
narrative.problemSolved: Designers version-controlled PSDs and Sketch files that developers could not easily inspect.
